summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived overview of Santa Monica, California, covering its early Asian American communities, its Tongva and Spanish-era history including the two competing accounts of its name, its bicycle infrastructure and advocacy, and the Douglas Aircraft Company's ties to Clover Field and the 1924 aerial circumnavigation attempt. The sections are loosely connected historical and modern snapshots of the city rather than a single narrative.
one_line: Wikipedia-based overview of Santa Monica, California, covering its early Asian American communities, Tongva and Spanish history, cycling initiatives, and Douglas Aircraft ties.
key_facts: Around the start of the 20th century, a growing population of Asian Americans lived in or near Santa Monica and Venice.
A Japanese fishing village was located near the Long Wharf, and Japanese village fishermen were an integral economic part of the Santa Monica Bay community.
Santa Monica was long inhabited by the Tongva people, and was called Kecheek in the Tongva language.
Explorer Gaspar de Portolà's party was the first non-indigenous group to set foot in the area, camping near the present day intersection of Barrington and Ohio Avenues on August 3, 1769.
One version says Santa Monica was named for the feast day of Saint Monica (mother of Saint Augustine), but her feast day is actually May 4.
Another version says Juan Crespí named the city after the Kuruvungna Springs (Serra Springs), which were reminiscent of the tears Saint Monica shed over her son's early impiety.
Santa Monica launched a bicycle sharing system in November 2015 and has a bike action plan.
The Marvin Braude Bike Trail traverses the city.
Santa Monica received the League of American Bicyclists' Bicycle Friendly Community Award at Bronze in 2009 and Silver in 2013.
Santa Monica Spoke is a local chapter of the Los Angeles County Bicycle Coalition.
Donald Wills Douglas, Sr. built a plant in 1922 at Clover Field (Santa Monica Airport) for the Douglas Aircraft Company.
In 1924, four Douglas-built planes took off from Clover Field to attempt the first aerial circumnavigation of the world.
Two planes made it back after covering 27,553 miles (44,342 km) in 175 days, and were greeted on September 23, 1924, by a crowd of 200,000 (generously estimated).
The Douglas Company (later McDonnell Douglas) kept facilities in the city until the 1960s.
